rv.q: It’s a mess, but it’s a big, fun Technicolor mess.
Welcome to this unsteady but audacious show.
It's not the thin gruel some had feared, but it's also not a spicy knock out — at least not yet.
Bartlett Sher, Theater's resident director, has done his best to make interesting things happen onstage, but the results are scatty and unfocused from start to finish.
As a musical, it has no buoyancy, with comedic plot lines deflating in translation and underdeveloped characters scurrying about — often on conveyer belts — without engendering much affection.
This musical adaptation of Pedro Almodovar's 1988 film never finds its footing.
Packed with talent and creativity, and a cast and crew bristling with Tony Awards, "Women on the Verge of a Nervous Breakdown" is nonetheless a sad casualty of its own wandering mind.
Despite the insistent beat of David Yazbek’s Spanish-accented score, however, the show can’t find a rhythm.
No one is helped by Yazbek's songs, which sound like Latin-flavored Muzak.
The songs themselves are pleasant enough, but they don't advance the plot or develop the characters in meaningful ways, and they frequently stop the show dead in its tracks.

Since theatergoing America apparently grows less knowledgeable by the day, After the Revolution should be viewed as, at worst, a useful clarifier, while its cast and the passion behind Herzog's writing often make it considerably more than that.
But what was funny and stylish in the movie is a frantic, unfocused mess here.
But seldom has such a strong cast been used to such poor effect.
Instead, it has turned out to be a hot mess of the highest pedigree.
Fans of the 1988 movie who thought the film would make great sense as a tuner will be baffled at how the skillfully crafted, hilarious flick has deteriorated into such a nearly incoherent shambles.
But the chief culprits are Lane’s scattershot book and Yazbek’s ho-hum songs, not one of them memorable.
For all its woes, "Women" does stand out in one way.
A yummy confection of silly romantic comedy, seductive Latin music, alluring visuals and high-powered performances.
Songs like 'Model Behavior', 'Yesterday, Tomorrow and Today', 'Tangled,' and 'Invisible' are gems that will stay with you.
They all try valiantly to rescue this piece of sludge, a show that is so mis-organized that it’s almost like an SAT test to try and re-order the scenes to make the show make sense.

cn.t: Critics find this starry musical adaptation a frantic, bloated mess that wastes exceptional talent from LuPone, Benanti, and Mitchell. Despite some entertaining moments and standout songs, the show fails to coalesce into a coherent whole.

sg.ra: Belasco was designed by David Belasco as a 'living room' with a shallow depth to support the Little Theater movement's emphasis on actor-audience proximity. Center Orchestra rows B-D sit at the ideal distance (reviewers cite row B as the fourth row from stage at 'perfect distance') with head-on actor views. Mezzanine overhang begins at row J per SeatPlan, so rows BB-H stay clear.

SeatPlan confirms 'The Mezzanine overhang begins at row J, meaning seats behind this may experience cut-off at the top of the stage.' Rows J-Q trade top-of-stage visibility for lower prices. Headout and TickPick both flag G-P/F-O center as value picks. Row N's extra legroom offsets the overhang compromise for tall patrons.

SeatPlan: 'Seats at the Left and Right edges suffer from restricted views of the stage,' particularly corner seats in rows B-E. TickPick confirms 'Far Left/Right Orchestra: Angled views may occur.' Historic box configuration and shallow house geometry amplify side-angle distortion.

sg.vl: Aerial sweet spot, skip row A
sg.ra: Mezzanine hangs close and center row C delivers aerial perspective with decent rake. Row A is a common trap: 'Mezzanine row A seat 111 was obstructed view, and the rail literally blocks half of the stage' (Tripadvisor user report). Balcony overhang begins at mezz row C per SeatPlan, so rows A-B stay open-topped but row A's safety bar offsets that benefit.

Headout flags F-H center as the mezzanine value range. Balcony overhang starting at row C means rows E-H sit under it — top of set may be cut. Side mezzanine suffers progressively more restricted angles 'due to stage curvature' (SeatPlan). Acceptable for dialogue-heavy work but not flown spectacle.

Center Balcony 'extends back six rows on a steep rake which provides a bird's-eye-view of the stage' (SeatPlan). Rows B-D balance price and sightline. Distance is the honest tradeoff: AVFMS reviewer on Maybe Happy Ending noted 'the real problem is how far back the balcony is. You'll have to lean forward to see for most of the show.' Row A safety rail can also obstruct.

sg.vl: Up to 1/3 of stage cut off
sg.ra: SeatPlan: 'the curve of the section and other features including the Left Boxes may cut off up to a third of the stage at the outside.' Combined with steep rake, distance, and row A rail, side balcony is the worst seat class in the house. Historic 1907 box architecture is the root cause — it cannot be engineered out per production.
